titulo: Beyls: Wrapping up LLVM's relicensing effort
resumo: Kristof Beyls has published a summary to the LLVM discussion forum to announce that the project is declaring success and bringing its relicensing effort to a close after eight years. We've been asking past contributors to relicense their work since 2018. New contributions have come in under Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception since January 19, 2019. Code contributed before that date was under LLVM's earlier licenses (UIUC/NCSA, plus MIT for some runtime libraries), so we needed permission from its authors to move it over. [...] Today, more than 99.5% of all lines of code ever contributed to LLVM are either covered by the new license, too small for copyright to apply, or no longer in the repository. Rather than trying to " chase the last tiny fraction forever " LLVM is winding up the effort. Any contributors with code contributed before January 19, 2019 who have not signed a relicensing agreement and do not want their contributions made available under Apache-2.0 with the LLVM-exception can still reach out to the project to ensure their code has the appropriate SPDX license identifier.

titulo: What to expect from DDR6, the next generation of RAM
resumo: Future PCs and servers are getting a pretty big memory upgrade. The standards body JEDEC has revealed new details ( via Techpowerup ) about DDR6, the next-generation memory standard. According to the preliminary specifications, the transfer rate for DDR6 RDIMMs will start at 12.8 billion transfers per second, compared with 9.2 billion for DDR5 RDIMMs. In the longer term, the aim is to reach 14.4 billion transfers per second or more. At the same time, the data bus will expand from 64 to 96 bits. Combined with the higher speeds, this is expected to deliver over 50 percent higher memory bandwidth. That said, this doesn’t mean programs and games will automatically run that much faster. DDR6 will also support higher-capacity memory chips with improved energy efficiency, alongside shorter memory modules measuring 74 mm. That’s down from the current 133 mm for DDR5. The standard is still under development, and the specifications are subject to change. JEDEC has yet to announce when the first DDR6 memory modules will launch.
